Thursday. It happened again in the corridor when someone else burned the same kind. Ira went rigid and said, "Can we go out?" Aadhya just said, "Sure," and didn't ask.

Ira looked up for a long moment. "Thanks. I honestly don't know why it does."

Charu, you asked how to live with a roommate you don't fully understand. When I was nineteen, in the women's hostel in Pune, I shared a room with Meenal. Lovely girl. But if anyone said, "Don't make a scene," even as a joke, she went stiff as a board and snapped at whoever spoke next.
I wanted to know why. Oh, how I wanted to know! But I only said to her once, quietly, "That phrase seems to upset you. I won't use it." She said, "I can't tell you why." I said, "You don't have to."
We shared that room for three years. She never told me, and I never asked again. At my wedding, Meenal was the first to arrive.
Your Rekha aunty has learnt a few things, you see.

qa.q: What phrase made Meenal go stiff?
qa.a: "Don't make a scene."

qa.q: Why did young Rekha want so badly to know the reason?
qa.a: Rekha was curious and probably wanted to help, but she chose to put Meenal's comfort ahead of her own need to understand.

qa.q: What choice did Rekha make that kept the friendship strong?
qa.a: Naming the reaction kindly once, promising not to use the phrase, and never digging for a story Meenal hadn't offered.

qa.q: What might Meenal arriving first at the wedding say about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests Meenal felt deeply respected by Rekha's restraint, and that the friendship meant a great deal to her.

The power had gone out at ten, the night before their final exam, and the two roommates were studying by one rechargeable lamp in their tiny Hyderabad flat. Jatin, frazzled, muttered, "Useless, useless," at his own notes.
Across the table Ramesh went rigid. "Can you not say that word," he said sharply, and shoved his chair back so hard it scraped.
Jatin stared. Ramesh never snapped. There was no time for a long talk and no other room to escape to. So Jatin said, "Sorry. I'll drop it," and turned the lamp a little toward Ramesh's side.
After a while Ramesh said, "I don't even know why it gets to me."
"You don't have to know," Jatin said. "Pass the highlighter?"

Dear diary, Kamal here. Something odd again with Raghav.

The cleaning staff did the corridor with that strong phenyl today. The minute Raghav walked in, he stopped, jaw tight, and said, "Close the door. Now." Then he snapped at me for leaving my shoes out, which he never cares about.

This is maybe the fourth time. Phenyl. Also once when the canteen guy said, "Hurry up, you're wasting everyone's time." Same freeze.

I don't know what it is. I have theories, but they're mine, not his.

Tonight I just said, "The phenyl days seem rough for you. I'll keep the window open." He looked at me for a second and nodded. He didn't explain. I didn't ask.

I think that's right. If he wants to tell me one day, he will.

Aiko didn't know what to do. She felt bad, but also confused.

When he came back, she said, "I noticed the smell really upset you. I'll be careful with toast."

Emeka looked at the floor. "I don't know why it does that."

"You don't have to explain," she said. "Want tea?"

He nodded. She didn't ask any more questions. Later he thanked her for not making it a big deal.
